title: The Iliad: Apollo's Plague
subtitle: A priest, a ransom, and a king's insult that starts it all

learningObjectives.text: Why does Apollo send the plague on the Greek camp?
What does Agamemnon demand for returning Chryseis?

main.author: Homer
main.locator: Iliad 1, Chryses petitions and Agamemnon refuses; Book 1, normalized characters 421-1518
main.excerpt: It was the son of Jove and Leto; for he was angry with the king and sent a pestilence upon the host to plague the people, because the son of Atreus had dishonoured Chryses his priest. Now Chryses had come to the ships of the Achaeans to free his daughter, and had brought with him a great ransom: moreover he bore in his hand the sceptre of Apollo wreathed with a suppliant’s wreath, and he besought the Achaeans, but most of all the two sons of Atreus, who were their chiefs. “Sons of Atreus,” he cried, “and all other Achaeans, may the gods who dwell in Olympus grant you to sack the city of Priam, and to reach your homes in safety; but free my daughter, and accept a ransom for her, in reverence to Apollo, son of Jove.” On this the rest of the Achaeans with one voice were for respecting the priest and taking the ransom that he offered; but not so Agamemnon, who spoke fiercely to him and sent him roughly away. “Old man,” said he, “let me not find you tarrying about our ships, nor yet coming hereafter. Your sceptre of the god and your wreath shall profit you nothing. I will not free her.

narrativeBlocks.title: A priest comes begging
narrativeBlocks.body: For nine days the Greek camp has been dying. Apollo's arrows — the plague itself — fell because Agamemnon refused a ransom: the priest Chryses came to buy back his daughter Chryseis, taken as a war-prize, and the king mocked and dismissed him.

narrativeBlocks.title: Achilles calls the assembly
narrativeBlocks.body: It is Achilles, not the king, who calls the army together and demands they ask a prophet why the god is angry. Calchas speaks: the plague will not lift until Chryseis goes home — unpaid, unransomed.

narrativeBlocks.title: The king's counter-demand
narrativeBlocks.body: Agamemnon gives way with a snarl: he will return the girl, but only if the army makes good his loss. 'I shall come to your tent and take your own prize' — someone's honour-prize will pay for his pride.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why a girl is a war-prize
narrativeBlocks.body: Chryseis is not a character with choices here; she is time — honour made physical. In the Greek camp, prizes measure a man's standing. Take one and you have not stolen property, you have publicly degraded a warrior.

narrativeBlocks.title: The quarrel that launches the epic
narrativeBlocks.body: The Iliad does not start with the war — it starts with this argument over honour. Everything that follows, every death including Patroclus and Hector, flows from this moment of wounded pride.

quiz.prompt: What does Agamemnon demand in exchange for releasing Chryseis?

choices.text: A ransom of seven tripods from the whole army
Achilles must publicly apologise to the priest
He will take another man's honour-prize to replace his — which means seizing Achilles's prize, Briseis
Immediate sacrifice of a hundred oxen to Apollo

quiz.explanation: Agamemnon agrees to return Chryseis but declares he will come to someone's tent and take their prize — the insult that provokes Achilles's withdrawal.

quiz.prompt: Why does Apollo send a plague on the Greek camp?

choices.text: The Greeks forgot a sacrifice before landing
The Trojans stole Apollo's sacred tripod
Agamemnon refused and mocked the priest Chryses, who came to ransom his daughter Chryseis

quiz.explanation: Chryses came to ransom his daughter; Agamemnon's insult moved Apollo to plague the host for nine days.
